name: Ming China
summary: The Han Chinese dynasty that drove out the Mongol Yuan. It built the Forbidden City and most of today’s Great Wall, and sent Zheng He’s great fleets across the Indian Ocean.

knownFor.label: Zheng He’s treasure fleets
knownFor.note: Huge voyages across the Indian Ocean.

knownFor.label: Great Wall (Ming)
knownFor.note: The brick wall most visitors see today.

location.value: China proper, ruling first from Nanjing, then from Beijing (designated capital in 1420). For a time it controlled Manchuria and occupied Vietnam (1406–1427).

terrain.value: The Yangtze valley (the main economic region), the North China Plain, and the Grand Canal, restored under Yongle. The Great Wall line ran along the northern frontier.

climate.value: The Little Ice Age brought cold and drought in the early 17th century, causing northern famines that fed rebellion.

resources.value: Rice, silk, cotton, tea and porcelain (Jingdezhen). crops from the Americas (maize, sweet potatoes, peanuts) arrived in the 16th century.

disasters.value: The 1556 Shaanxi earthquake, the deadliest earthquake on record (about 830,000 deaths). Yellow River floods. The Great Plague of 1633–1644.

population.value: About 65 million in 1393, 125 million in 1500 and 160 million in 1600 (Maddison 2006, via the Wikipedia infobox). Late-Ming estimates range up to 200 million because censuses missed tax evaders.

urbanisation.value: Beijing and Nanjing were huge walled capitals (the Nanjing wall was about 48 km long). Commercial cities flourished in the Yangtze delta.

disease.value: The Great Plague (1633–1644) spread from Zhejiang to Henan in the dynasty’s final years.

migration.value: Coastal people turned to smuggling and overseas trade despite the maritime bans (haijin). Settlers moved to frontier regions such as Yunnan.

economicBase.value: Agriculture plus booming commerce and crafts (porcelain, silk, cotton) in the 16th century.

tradeRoutes.value: Zheng He’s treasure fleets (1405–1433), then restrictions on private sea trade. Portuguese at Macau (from 1557) and Spanish silver via Manila supplied huge silver inflows.

wealth.value: GDP per person of about 19.8 taels, a decline from the Song (Broadberry 2014, via the Wikipedia infobox).

moneyAndTax.value: Paper money until about 1450, then it collapsed through inflation. Silver and copper coins took over. Zhang Juzheng’s Single Whip tax reforms (1570s). Silver price shocks in the 1630s–40s.

inequality.value: Land concentrated in tax-exempt estates of nobles, eunuchs and temples, while the tax burden fell on peasants.

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy. The Hongwu emperor abolished the chancellor post in 1380, and emperors ruled through the Grand Secretariat and the Six Ministries.

keyRulers.value: Hongwu (Zhu Yuanzhang, 1368–1398). Yongle (1402–1424, moved the capital to Beijing, sent Zheng He). Wanli (1572–1620, withdrew from government for decades). Chongzhen (1627–1644, last).

succession.value: Hereditary. Yongle seized the throne from his nephew in a civil war (the Jingnan campaign, 1399–1402).

institutions.value: Civil service examinations with the “eight-legged essay” (from 1487; 24,874 jinshi degrees awarded over 276 years). The Embroidered Uniform Guard (secret police). Thirteen provinces.

stability.value: Purges under Hongwu (about 100,000 executed). The Tumu Crisis (1449), when the emperor was captured by the Oirats. Revolts in the 1620s–40s.

eliteConflict.value: Powerful eunuchs (e.g. Wei Zhongxian under Tianqi), and fierce factional conflict between the Donglin faction and its enemies.

armyAndTech.value: A standing army of over one million under Hongwu, organised in hereditary military households (weisuo). Firearms and cannon. The rebuilt brick-and-stone Great Wall.

majorWars.value: The Battle of Lake Poyang (1363), possibly the largest naval battle in history. The Tumu Crisis (1449). Wars against Japanese-led pirates. The Imjin War in Korea (1592–98). Wars with the Manchus from 1618.

territoryChange.value: About 6.5 million km² around 1450 (Wikipedia infobox). Withdrew from Vietnam in 1427 after Lê Lợi’s resistance. Lost Manchuria to the Later Jin (Qing).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals were the Mongols (Oirats), Japanese pirates, Japan under Hideyoshi, and the Manchus. Joseon Korea was an ally. A tributary system covered Korea, Ryukyu and much of Southeast Asia.

inventions.value: Shipbuilding for Zheng He’s fleets (Nanjing shipyards built about 2,000 vessels between 1403 and 1419). The rebuilt Great Wall, Forbidden City engineering, and gunpowder weapons. Private newspapers appeared in Beijing by 1582.

scienceEducation.value: Encyclopaedic works (the Yongle Encyclopedia, Song Yingxing’s Tiangong Kaiwu, 1637). Jesuits such as Matteo Ricci brought European science. Literacy rates are not stated in the sources checked.

openness.value: Mixed. It sent the great Zheng He voyages, then restricted private sea trade (haijin), but still absorbed American silver and crops and welcomed some Jesuit scholars.

communicationTransport.value: The Grand Canal rebuilt (1411–15); post stations; Zheng He’s treasure fleets (1405–1433).

religion.value: Confucianism, Buddhism (Hongwu had been a monk), Taoism (favoured by Jiajing), folk religion, Islam and early Catholicism.

languageWriting.value: Mandarin as the official spoken standard. Classical and vernacular Chinese in a booming print culture.

artsArchitecture.value: The Forbidden City in Beijing (1406–1420) and most of today’s visible Great Wall. Classic novels (Water Margin, Journey to the West). Painters such as Shen Zhou and Wen Zhengming. Blue-and-white porcelain.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Ming dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: Ming Great Wall (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

socialStructure.value: Emperor, scholar-gentry, merchants growing in wealth, peasants, hereditary military and artisan households, and eunuchs at court.

sharedIdentity.value: Presented itself as restoring Han Chinese rule after the Mongol Yuan.

dailyLife.value: Courtyard houses; rice, wheat noodles, pork and vegetables; tea for everyone.

neighbours.value: Admiral Zheng He’s treasure fleets (1405–1433) sailed to Southeast Asia (including Melaka), India, Arabia and the Swahili coast of East Africa. Neighbours included Joseon, Japan, the Mongols and Đại Việt.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Zheng He (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

ideasReligions.value: Jesuit missionaries (Ricci) introduced European maps and mathematics. Columbian Exchange crops arrived. Chinese porcelain was exported worldwide (about 16% of late-Ming ceramic exports went to Europe).

colonisation.value: Occupied Vietnam (1406–1427) and absorbed Yunnan (1381). Relations with Tibet are debated: historians disagree whether they amounted to sovereignty or loose religious and diplomatic ties.

riseSignals.value: Zhu Yuanzhang led the Red Turban rebels against the failing Yuan. Defeated rivals at Lake Poyang (1363) and took Nanjing. Strong early government under Hongwu and Yongle.

peakPeriod.value: The Yongle reign (1402–1424): Zheng He’s voyages, the new capital at Beijing, and the Yongle Encyclopedia.

declineSignals.value: Eunuch power and factionalism, an absent emperor (Wanli), costly wars (Korea 1592–98), a silver crisis, the Little Ice Age, famine and plague, military desertions, and the rise of the Manchus.

outcome.value: Fell in 1644 when Li Zicheng’s rebels took Beijing and the Chongzhen emperor died by suicide. Wu Sangui let the Manchus through the Shanhai Pass, and the Qing took over. Southern Ming regimes lasted until 1662.

sources.value: The History of Ming (compiled under the Qing, possibly censored), the Veritable Records, local gazetteers, and European accounts. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Brook (2010) and Mote (1999).

overallCertainty.value: Good for politics. Population (160–200 million) and GDP are estimates. The Beijing capital date is given as 1403 (designation) or 1420/1421 (formal move). Some topics, like Tibet and social mobility through exams, are debated.
